items.title: Kingdom Hearts Is a Billion-Dollar Franchise, Disney Declares Ahead of Hotly Anticipated D23 Panel
items.description: Kingdom Hearts is one of nine billion-dollar franchises Disney has under its video game banner.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Kingdom Hearts is one of nine billion-dollar franchises Disney has under its video game banner.

The news comes ahead of a hotly anticipated panel at D23, where Disney is expected to talk about Kingdom Hearts 4.

In a blog post, Disney said its Disney Games Group portfolio “spans nine billion-dollar franchises including Kingdom Hearts and Marvel Strike Force.” More than half of these billion-dollar franchises have come out in the last 12 years.

Disney games have driven an estimated $3.5 billion in consumer spend annually for the past four years — and crossed $4 billion this past fiscal year, Disney said. That includes all Marvel games, all Star Wars games, indeed all games based on any Disney IP, of which there are many.

Upcoming Disney games include Marvel’s Wolverine, from Insomniac, the Iron Man game from EA’s Motive, and Star Wars Eclipse from Quantic Dream, although there is a cloud hanging over the latter. Meanwhile, Disney is also the rights holder for Respawn’s Star Wars Jedi 3, Creative Assembly’s Alien: Isolation 2, and Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra.

Kingdom Hearts’ name on Disney's billion-dollar list perhaps comes as a surprise, given how few mainline entires have been released since Kingdom Hearts released in 2002 for the PlayStation 2. It suggests Kingdom Hearts games really do sell well, and goes some way to explaining the anticipation for Kingdom Hearts 4.

Speaking of which, a livestream of the ‘DEEP DIVE into KINGDOM HEARTS panel at D23’ will be available on August 15 at 4.30pm PT / 7.30pm ET / August 16 at 12.30am UK time. Disney said it will offer a “behind-the-scenes look at the making of the games,” but it’s who’s on the panel that has fans excited for what is now expected news on Kingdom Hearts 4.

The panel guests are Nana Gadd from Disney & Pixar Games, Tai Yasue from Square Enix, Haley Joel Osment, who voices Sora, David Gallagher, who voices Riku, and Renée Johnson, who is behind the Disney character voices. With a panel like that (Yasue is believed to be co-director of Kingdom Hearts 4), you’d like to think we’ll get something on the hotly anticipated sequel.

Kingdom Hearts 4 made a surprise appearance at the June 2026 Nintendo Direct to reveal a first look at gameplay years after the game itself was announced. In a separate post, Square Enix confirmed that Kingdom Hearts 4 will launch simultaneously for PC via Epic Games Store and Steam, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S, as well as Nintendo Switch 2.

"A new installment in the action role-playing series developed and published by Square Enix, Kingdom Hearts 4 gives fans a look at some of the characters that protagonist Sora will meet in the mysterious city of Quadratum," an official description for the game said. "Sora will once again journey to realms, where new figures cross his path and new powers awaken his next chapter. Kingdom Hearts 4 will be available at launch on Nintendo Switch 2."

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

items.title: Sony Wants to Create an Original Character IP to Rival Hello Kitty — and a Stressed-Out Insomniac Bear Is in the Running
items.description: Japanese character goods, like Hello Kitty, are popular worldwide for their cute and recognizable designs. Now, Sony is entering the fray. Sony Creative Products (SCP), the division that manages the Sony Group’s character IPs, wants to develop its own characters with universal appeal that can generate 10 billion yen (approx. $62.8 million) in annual sales by 2030.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Japanese character goods, like Hello Kitty, are popular worldwide for their cute and recognizable designs. Now, Sony is entering the fray. Sony Creative Products (SCP), the division that manages the Sony Group’s character IPs, wants to develop its own characters with universal appeal that can generate 10 billion yen (approx. $62.8 million) in annual sales by 2030.

As reported by Nikkei, the aim is to create original characters that Sony can make merchandise and multimedia centered around. To this end, it has established a dedicated team tasked with creating potential hit characters, and even opened a special event space in Tokyo.

Living in Japan, you really can’t escape from mascot characters and their merchandise. Chances are your nearest bank, supermarket or fast food chain is doing some kind of collaboration with some recognizable bug-eyed cutie. Many companies, cities and prefectures have their own mascot characters (the best known is probably Kumamoto prefecture’s Kumamon). Then there’s the major player in character goods: Sanrio, home of the world-famous Hello Kitty and a whole stable of fluffy icons including Kuromi, Cinnamoroll, and Pompom Purin. There’s also San-X, the creator of Rirakuma, and the Sumikko Gurashi family of characters.

Now, Sony is aiming to take on this market with new original characters of its own. Currently in the running is Nemu the Night Owl Bear, who has racked up over 1 million followers in a year. Created in collaboration with Tokyo-based company Tsumupapa, Nemu is a bear character who worries so much about life’s problems that he struggles to sleep. According to a SCP executive officer Nikkei interviewed, this “stress-filled society theme is resonating across borders,” with the bear apparently gaining much popularity in South Korea. Further plans for merchandise and an anime featuring Nemu are currently in the works.

Sony’s goal of 10 billion yen in annual sales by 2030 for original IP characters is a comparatively high one. For context, a character in Japan is usually considered a hit if its merchandise racks up between 2~3 billion yen in annual sales, according to SCP. However, with the Sony Group’s broad reach across anime, music, game and film, an original mascot (or two) already has many potential avenues to score fans and generate revenue.

As for the video game sector, while Nintendo has Mario and Sega has Sonic, Sony has always struggled to find an enduring mascot. If you ask gamers who Sony’s mascot is, their answer will probably depend on which PlayStation generation they grew up with. They might say Crash Bandicoot, Sackboy, or Astrobot. Then there are the many human characters from one-time PlayStation exclusives that became associated with the brand (Lara Croft, Solid Snake, Kratos, Nathan Drake et al.). There’s also Toro Inoue, the white cat from the Doko Demo Issyo series who became a PlayStation mascot in Japan for a while. However, Toro lacks the widespread international recognition that Nintendo’s plumber and Sega’s blue hedgehog enjoy.

The current issue is that Sony suffers from a lack of fully-owned, recognizable original characters, and the SCP aims to address this. It has a track record in handling domestic events for popular character IPs owned by other companies, and for revitalizing specific IPs in Japan, like the Peanuts comic strip characters (Snoopy and co.), which it acquired in March 2026. SCP is also using technology to enhance peoples’ encounters with such characters at events.

To this end, Sony Creative Products opened the Yurakucho Museum in Tokyo. This space aims to provide immersive character-related exhibitions. Currently, SCP is using haptics to enhance a Pingu exhibition, including vibrating floors and gusts of wind. Sony holds the marketing rights to Pingu in Japan, and doubled the Swiss-born penguin character’s merchandise sales in the country last year (source: Mainichi).

But can Sony apply its marketing successes with well-known character IPs to its own brand new, original creations? Could we get tie-in anime series and games with some cute new Sony characters? Watch this space.

Image credit: Tsumupapa.

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

items.title: Project Revenant, a Unique Precision-Aiming 2D Sidescroller, Announces Public Playtest
items.description: Korea-based developer Mayfly is developing Project Revenant, a unique 2D sidescrolling action game for PC where you'll need to use your mouse to specifically target enemies in order to hit them. No spray-and-pray here!
items.author: Ryan McCaffrey
items.content:
Korea-based developer Mayfly is developing Project Revenant, a unique 2D sidescrolling action game for PC where you'll need to use your mouse to specifically target enemies in order to hit them. No spray-and-pray here! Watch the new trailer above and check out almost two dozen gameplay screenshots in the gallery below.

"This is not a game where you can spray bullets and hope for the best," the developers said. "To survive, you must master the unique combat system known as 'Precision Aiming,' where only enemies directly under your cursor will take damage. This is not a game where you can spray bullets and hope for the best. You’ll need to carefully analyze each enemy’s position and attack pattern, then strike with accuracy. Headshot an enemy to take them out instantly, shoot down a chandelier to crush enemies beneath it, or ignite an explosive barrel to wipe out a group of foes. Every encounter is a tactical decision."

Project Revenant promises unique gameplay twists on every stage, unique bosses, a wide variety of enemies such as cyborg ninjas, giant robots, and bounty hunters, and varied environments. Check it out for yourself in the playtest beginning on August 26 on Steam.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked, and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch. He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: War in the North Dev Warned Warner Bros. Not to Go Up Against Skyrim Back in 2011
items.description: The Lord of the Rings: War in the North developer "argued vociferously" not to go up against Skyrim, but he was "overruled."
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Cast your mind back to November 2011, and two big fantasy games based on established IPs came out pretty much at the same time: Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, which went on to sell over 65 million copies, and Snowblind Studios’ The Lord of the Rings: War in the North, which failed commercially.

In retrospect, it was perhaps unwise for publisher Warner Bros. to release The Lord of the Rings: War in the North in the same week as Skyrim, given the extreme hype Bethesda’s behemoth enjoyed ahead of launch. But that’s exactly what Warner Bros. did — despite, it seems, the advice not to do so that it received from at least one high-ranking developer it had on its books.

Christian Allen was the design director on the WB Games Seattle leadership team at the time, working on the likes of Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max, and F.E.A.R. 2: Reborn. He noticed this week’s surprise Aspyr-developed re-release of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North across PC and console, and it sparked something of a trip down memory lane.

In a series of tweets, Allen said that he tried to convince the powers that be at Warner Bros. to avoid Skyrim for obvious reasons, but he was “overruled.”

“Wow, this is cool,” he began. “15 years ago I argued vociferously not to release this up against Skyrim, as it wouldn't get a fair shake. I got overruled. Nice to see it get a proper release.”

Why did Warner Bros. make such an obviously risky decision here? Allen added some context: “Quarterly revenue motivations drive more decisions than people realize. It's a big challenge with stock-price driven organizations. Must be hard to be an exec and go, ‘Well, this game will do better if we hold it until March, but my bonus will take a 50% hit.’”

Allen went on to talk about the impact Skyrim had on the visibility of Snowblind’s game. “At the time it really seemed to get lost in the wash, and every review just compared it to Skyrim (as I predicted they would),” he said.

“I think it only got like one review the week it launched,” he continued. “IIRC there was hardly any marketing, either they wrote it off or thought hardcore LOTR fans would just know about it, somehow.”

Following the failure of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North, Snowblind was merged with Monolith Productions, which went on to release Gotham City Impostors, Guardians of Middle-earth, and the much-loved Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor and Middle-earth: Shadow of War.

Last year, Warner Bros. closed Monolith down, having canceled its Wonder Woman video game. Allen is now design director on Steam hit Project Zomboid.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

items.title: Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse Suffers Significant Leak Online as 4 Minutes of Footage Hits Social Media
items.description: The hotly anticipated Spider-Man: Beyond The Spider-Verse has suffered a significant leak, with four minutes of footage hitting social media today.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
The hotly anticipated Spider-Man: Beyond The Spider-Verse has suffered a significant leak, with four minutes of footage hitting social media today.

Sony is currently battling to scrub the footage from the likes of X / Twitter, but it faces an uphill challenge as users share the clip across multiple social channels.

The footage, which appears to be from the opening of the animated movie, also includes a trailer montage that points to the current June 18, 2027 release date. It is thought this is the footage shown behind closed doors at CinemaCon earlier this year.

This is the latest video leak Sony and indeed Marvel have suffered in recent years, with everything from Tom Holland’s Spider-Man films to Avengers: Doomsday content leaking all over the internet.

Beyond The Spider-Verse, directed by Bob Persichetti and Justin K. Thompson, with a story written by Phil Lord, Christopher Miller, and David Callaham, is the final chapter of Sony Pictures Animation's Oscar-winning Spider-Verse saga. It follows 2018's Into the Spider-Verse and 2023's Across the Spider-Verse. If the animated movie hits its current release date, it’ll arrive four years after Across the Spider-Verse and eight years after Into the Spider-Verse came out.

Here’s the official description:

Hunted by Miguel O’Hara’s Spider Society and betrayed by his friends, Miles finds himself in the darkest corners of the Spider-Verse in search of a way home. Knowing that his family has been not only fractured but endangered by his calling, it’s a race against the clock for Miles to travel across the wildest reaches of time and space to fight for and reunite everything he holds most dear.

Speaking to Variety in March, Lord and Miller insisted Beyond the Spider-Verse was on track, calling the movie the “most emotional” film in the trilogy. “It’s on schedule and it’s going to be beautiful and emotional,” Lord said. “I would say the most emotional of the three,” Miller added. He went on to talk about the new ways Spot is being animated.

Warning! Spoilers for the Spider-Verse movies follow:

Dr. Johnathon Ohnn, aka the Spot, is the main antagonist of the Spider-Verse movies. The former Alchemax scientist was transformed into a portal-creating supervillain when Miles Morales destroyed Kingpin’s Super-Collider. Spot is really, really angry at Miles, who he blames for ruining his life. And at the end of Across the Spider-Verse, after becoming incredibly powerful, he sets out to murder Miles' father, Jefferson Davis.

Spot steals pretty much every scene he’s in, with his wonderfully animated portal power fuelling increasingly elaborate, mind-bending action scenes. “... there are some new things they’re developing for the look… of what Spot does specifically that are extra amazing,” Miller said, teasing even more Spot mayhem.

“They’re really extraordinary. They’re going to be great,” Lord said, adding: “... artistically… It’s going to take you to places of abstraction that I think are going to be really special.”

In February, Lord and Miller explained why Beyond the Spider-Verse was taking so long. They said that a lot of the delay had to do with the pressure they put on themselves to outdo the previous two movies, which enjoyed critical and commercial acclaim, and the sheer amount of work required to come up with something that would do just that. Then there were issues that came with the decision to split the sequel in two, and subsequently having to piece it back together to create not just a coherent trilogy, but coherent individual movies.

“At one point it was one movie, but there was too much movie there, so it was separated into two,” Miller told io9. “But then once you looked at that second half of a movie, you’re like, ‘Well, that’s like not just a story arc that has a beginning, middle, and end.”

“We know where it’s headed, but we need to understand better what’s happening in the middle,” Lord added. “And we came upon a really wonderful notion, which is when your family is broken apart by your calling, your talents, how do you put them back together? How do you have it all?”

“We put the most pressure on ourselves,” Miller went on to say. “There’s no one that puts more pressure on us than ourselves, wanting to outdo ourselves each time and see things that you haven’t seen before and make it feel like something you’ve never experienced before. And so, trying to get something that is as worthy as the previous two has been the driver.”

“Having to take it apart to put it back together again was really, really [the] real thing that made it take longer,” Miller said.

Daniel Kaluuya, who played Hobart "Hobie" Brown / Spider-Punk in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, is set to play the same character in Beyond the Spider-Verse (he’s also set to reprise the role in a Spider-Punk animated spinoff). Marvin Jones III, who voices supervillain Tombstone in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, is also set to reprise his role for Beyond the Spider-Verse.

In February, Lord and Miller explained why Beyond the Spider-Verse was taking so long. They said that a lot of the delay had to do with the pressure they put on themselves to outdo the previous two movies, which enjoyed critical and commercial acclaim, and the sheer amount of work required to come up with something that would do just that. Then there were issues that came with the decision to split the sequel in two, and subsequently having to piece it back together to create not just a coherent trilogy, but coherent individual movies.

“At one point it was one movie, but there was too much movie there, so it was separated into two,” Miller told io9. “But then once you looked at that second half of a movie, you’re like, ‘Well, that’s like not just a story arc that has a beginning, middle, and end.”

“We know where it’s headed, but we need to understand better what’s happening in the middle,” Lord added. “And we came upon a really wonderful notion, which is when your family is broken apart by your calling, your talents, how do you put them back together? How do you have it all?”

“We put the most pressure on ourselves,” Miller went on to say. “There’s no one that puts more pressure on us than ourselves, wanting to outdo ourselves each time and see things that you haven’t seen before and make it feel like something you’ve never experienced before. And so, trying to get something that is as worthy as the previous two has been the driver.”

“Having to take it apart to put it back together again was really, really [the] real thing that made it take longer,” Miller said.

Daniel Kaluuya, who played Hobart "Hobie" Brown / Spider-Punk in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, is set to play the same character in Beyond the Spider-Verse (he’s also set to reprise the role in a Spider-Punk animated spinoff). Marvin Jones III, who voices supervillain Tombstone in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, is also set to reprise his role for Beyond the Spider-Verse.

items.title: The X-Files Creator Chris Carter Wants to Continue the Story on From the Divisive Season 11 Finale
items.description: IGN interviews Chris Carter on The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn and finally continuing the mainline story.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Chris Carter knows The X-Files isn’t finished. At least, the story isn’t finished. Some believe The X-Files finally came to an end on March 21, 2018, following its Season 11 finale. But that episode, My Struggle IV, ended on a reveal that, clearly, was meant to be explored further — even as it divided fans. The question is, will Chris Carter, who created the much-loved alien conspiracy thriller back in the early ‘90s, get the chance?

I interviewed Carter to talk about the release of The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn, his Director’s Cut of the second X-Files movie. As a veteran X-Files fan, I appreciated the opportunity to return to the world of 1998 and Mulder and Scully doing monster of the week things for an hour-and-a-half. As our The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn review says, this new, horror-leaning version of the movie won’t change anyone’s mind about it. But it certainly left me wondering about what’s next for Carter and his The X-Files.

So, what is next? Carter told me he has a “big reveal” for fans and really does want to make it a reality, but it sounds unclear if that will be via a new The X-Files TV series or a movie. Certainly nothing is greenlit. All the while, a new version of The X-Files is in the works. Sinners and Black Panther director Ryan Coogler has filmed a pilot for an The X-Files reboot for Hulu. Will that feature Mulder and Scully in some way? If it does, does that make it canon to Carter’s show?

For now, we have The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn to fuss over, and Carter’s masterplan for his story to ponder. The interview in full is below.

IGN: I had watched the original version, I've watched your new version, and I'd love to pick your brains a little bit about some of the changes you've made and why you've made them.

Chris Carter: The reason I wanted to go back and do this is, when we made the movie and showed it to the studio for the first time, the executives kind of tore us a new one. They actually referred to it as torture porn, as if it were a Saw movie. They said, "This isn't a PG-13 movie that you promised to make for us." And they made us cut it back to what they believed was a PG-13 movie. And so we made that hurdle.

But the next hurdle was unexpected. Whoever the governing body is that makes the rules on ratings said, "This isn't a PG-13 movie," and we had to cut it back even further. And so I felt like we had to cut a lot of the things that I thought made it an X-File. And ironically, I could do more on an hour of television than I could do with this standards and practices, the censors, than I could do for a PG-13 movie. So I always felt the movie got cut back and didn't really meet the standards of a good, scary X-Files. That's basically the reason I wanted to do this.

IGN: And so what changes have you made and why have you made them?

Chris Carter: So it's funny, people say usually a Director's Cut, it's what's added back in, all the additional material. I've actually cut it back. And one of the reasons for that, I actually cut down on the Mulder and Scully, call it romantic line, because we had had two reboots in between, and I felt like people got a lot of Mulder and Scully romance in those two reboots. And so coming back to this movie, I wanted to cut that back and focus on the scary stuff.

IGN: What scary stuff did you want to add in?

Chris Carter: It's really more the Frankenstein story, which is why I've added this new title to it. I always felt like it wasn't appreciated as a Frankenstein story, and it's only nodded to at the end of the movie. The idea that came to me, the reason for this movie was I read about a doctor who had transplanted the head of a monkey onto another monkey. And I loved it. I thought that's X-File's territory right there. I actually sought this man out in Cleveland, Ohio. I flew out there and got to sit with him at Case Western University and talk to him about the actual surgery. It was successful. The monkey ended up dying, but it was a successful head transplant. And that really was the idea behind I Want to Believe.

I Want to Believe, actually, the title, which comes right from the X-Files series, really informed the movie and the storytelling. But even more so, the beating heart of the show was ‘Don't Give Up.’ And that came because of a... I had gone to a talk with a very smart, soulful man named Huston Smith, who's no longer with us. I went to a talk that he gave, and he's a religious scholar, and he just took us all over with his experiences, his learning, his beliefs. And so it was about an hour-and-a-half of him completely entrancing us. And at the end of his talk, somebody raised their hand and said, "If you could sum up your experiences and knowledge in a sentence, what would it be?" And I cringed. I thought, oh my gosh, this man has just imparted all of this wisdom, and this person's asking for the bumper sticker.

And he thought about it, kind of looked up to the stars, and looked back and said, "Don't give up." And I thought, that's it. That's the secret to life itself. And I had to put that in the movie because I felt that it is the secret. Now, it could also be something reduced to a Nike t-shirt, but I thought there was such wisdom in those three words.

IGN: In 2026, how relevant do you feel The X-Files is?

Chris Carter: I'm going to tell you, I think it is relevant because everyone keeps telling me it's relevant. There's a huge hardcore fanbase out there, and bless their hearts, they've adopted Mulder and Scully. I think it's really those two characters are the secret to our success. Their relationship wasn't just romantic. It's respectful. It is combative. It is, for me, my perfect idea of a romance, of a relationship, of a friendship, of a mutually respectful relationship. And I think that's simply the reason that people are still drawn to the show.

I think we told great stories. I think great people came to work on the show and made it better. And I was just visiting one of those people the other day, David Nutter, who came and directed some of our very best episodes. I'm working on something right now with Glen Morgan, who he and his partner, James Wong, wrote some of our best episodes and then directed some of them too. I'm still working with these people. Darin Morgan came in and wrote some of the funniest X-Files episodes ever. So it's not just good storytelling. It's not just Mulder and Scully. It is the inspiration that these people brought to the concept itself.

IGN: I know there's other X-Files things happening, but your story was clearly not finished based on the last season and how it ended with the pregnancy reveal. What's the plan?

Chris Carter: There were four episodes that I worked on, they were called My Struggle I, My Struggle II, III, and IV. And they were all a setup for where I imagined the series would go. I have a big reveal for everyone, and I'm excited to do that if we ever have another chance. Ryan Coogler is doing his version of The X-Files, and I don't want to do anything to spoil that, get in the way of that, affect that. So we'll give him that respect and that space that he deserves. But I do have something... I do have another story or a series or a movie in where I want to explore that storyline that I've set up so carefully.

The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn premieres on Disney+ and Hulu on August 14, 2026.

items.title: Xbox's Separation from Compulsion Games Seems Complete as Studio Is Listed as the Publisher of South of Midnight on Steam
items.description: Xbox's separation from Compulsion Games – one of four studios it spun out independently during the recent Xbox "reset" amidst thousands of layoffs – appears to be complete, as the developer itself is now listed as the publisher of 2025's award-winning South of Midnight on Steam instead of Xbox Game Studios.
items.author: Ryan McCaffrey
items.content:
Xbox's separation from Compulsion Games – one of four studios it spun out independently during the recent Xbox "reset" amidst thousands of layoffs – appears to be complete, as the developer itself is now listed as the publisher of 2025's award-winning South of Midnight on Steam instead of Xbox Game Studios. The change was first pointed out by indie developer Michael Klamerus on Bluesky. (Hat tip to IGN Discord member Tommy for flagging it to us.)

Interestingly, Xbox Game Studios is still listed as the publisher of Double Fine's Psychonauts 2 on Steam despite the San Francisco game developer also becoming independent after Xbox's recent sweeping changes. The same is also currently true for Undead Labs' State of Decay 3 and Ninja Theory's Senua, though both of those studios were acquired by other publishers who have yet to be revealed.

It's been a rough year for both Xbox employees and Xbox fans – including most recently tepid early sales numbers for Halo: Campaign Evolved – but there is at least some cool stuff to be optimistic about in the coming months, from Gears of War: E-Day's release in October (check out our multiplayer hands-on impressions – and the sick special-edition controllers) to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 giving us a break from Black Ops, the 10-out-of-10 Forza Horizon 6 pulling into PlayStation's driveway sometime before the end of the year, and Fable making its long-awaited return in February.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked, and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch. He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan.

items.title: Supergirl Featurette Wiped From YouTube After Fans Spot Director Using Alleged AI Concept Art for Lobo
items.description: Lobo’s intimidating design in Warner Bros.’ 2026 Supergirl film was seemingly made with the help of artificial intelligence, something that sparked backlash among fans and resulted in a video revealing the news to get wiped off YouTube.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
A featurette from Warner Bros. showed what appeared to be AI-generated concept art for Lobo's design in Supergirl, something that sparked backlash among fans and seemingly resulted in the video being wiped from YouTube.

Jason Momoa returned to the DCU as Lobo, decked out in white bodypaint, black leather, and a sinister grin befitting the bounty hunter. A featurette diving into Momoa’s performance was uploaded to YouTube after the film’s release in summer 2026, showing Supergirl director Craig Gillespie speaking to the actor while swiping through concept art on a laptop — artwork that seemed to be AI generated.

While only a few images of Lobo’s early look were shown at a distance, it’s impossible to ignore their resemblance to AI-generated content in terms of lighting and their overall soft, blurred look. Fans immediately clocked the similarities and took to the comments section to protest Gillespie’s apparent use of AI for such a massive feature film.

Director Craig Gillespie seemingly used AI generated concept "art" for ‘SUPERGIRL.’ pic.twitter.com/aU2h4oXHwr

— Nexus Point News (@NexusPointNews) August 13, 2026

The featurette was wiped from YouTube mere hours later. No official comment on the situation has yet been made by DC nor Warner Bros., leaving angry fans demanding answers. IGN has reached out to DC Studios for comment.

"Never hire Craig Gillespie again," one fan wrote on X.

"They got caught in 4k and panicked," another said of the video's removal.

"They noticed people where hating on the AI [sic] and took down the video," another suggested.

This is just the latest blow to hit Supergirl following its struggle at the box office in June. As of August 2026, it stands as one of the lowest-grossing DC Comics adaptations of all time, garnering $124 million globally on a $170 million budget. IGN’s Clint Gage scored it a 6 out of 10, saying it “borrows from the best, but Milly Alcock’s great take on Kara Zor-El gets lost in the spare parts from other movies used to assemble her story.”

Peter Safran's DC Studios and Gillespie also suffered from some creative clashes, reportedly testing competing cuts for Supergirl mere months before the film went to theaters. Sources close to the project told The Hollywood Reporter that the studio and Gillespie were "not creatively aligned,” and DC Studios’ version ended up winning out in the end.

Despite Supergirl’s lukewarm reception, Warner Bros. is still moving full speed ahead on James Gunn’s sequel to Superman, Man of Tomorrow, with WB chief David Zasla remarking in an interview with Deadline: “A handful of recent films have underperformed expectations. Media is, by nature, a business full of hits and misses.”

James Gunn's Superman, on the other hand, was far more warmly received, with IGN scoring the flick an 8 out of 10 for being a "wonderfully entertaining, heartfelt cinematic reset" for the DCU.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze.

items.title: Artist Behind Viral Spider-Man: Brand New Day Poster Forced to Take Drawing Down
items.description: The artist behind the viral, hand-drawn poster advertising Spider-Man: Brand New Day for has identified himself after his workplace forced him to take the drawing down.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
The artist behind the viral, hand-drawn poster advertising Spider-Man: Brand New Day for has identified himself after his workplace forced him to take the drawing down.

Drake Landon is the genius behind the hilarious illustration, who created it after the Cineplex theater where he worked didn’t receive an official poster to place on the outside of their business.

The adorable ‘Spooderman,’ as fans have taken to calling it, came with a humble apology explaining the situation. And while it proved to be a big hit online, his employer didn’t take too kindly to his proactive solution.

On August 12, a Reddit user claiming to be Landon made his first public post about the situation, saying he chose to reveal himself because “I honestly don't care at this point.”

He explained that his boss got called by Cineplex’s head office, which asked for the poster to be removed. Luckily, he was able to retrieve his artwork, which he plans on selling in limited amounts as prints or re-drawn duplicates.

“I have the poster back, sadly due to my boss telling me that head office called and asked for it to be taken down, for reasons that make sense now I realize. I don't wanna upset the studio, so yeah,” he wrote.

While it’s definitely a bummer (come on, corporate, don’t be sticks in the mud), Landon says his sudden popularity earned him a free booth at his local comic convention, where he plans on selling his other work — though he said it “probably won’t be as popular as Spooderman.”

Landon also shed some light on why he needed to make the poster in the first place, saying the distributor responsible for delivering the official materials accidentally sent them to the wrong location.

Despite this turn of events, Landon’s artwork proved that a creative solution to a sudden problem can open up all kinds of possibilities. Now if only Marvel would use this as an alternate cover for special Brand New Day Blu-ray editions of the movie…

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is still in theaters, and it’s been a hit at the box office. It managed to topple Avengers: Endgame to have the biggest domestic opening weekend in history is on track to cross $2 billion globally.

IGN’s Tom Jorgensen scored the flick a 7 out of 10, saying it “effectively refocuses on the most reliable pillars of the webslinger: battling inner turmoil, swinging around NYC saving the day, and looking cool while doing so.”

items.title: Night School Staff Speak Out After Netflix Shuts Down Developer Following 'Top Tier' Launch of Unhinged
items.description: Netflix is shuttering its Los Angeles-based game studio Night School, best known for side-scrolling psychological thrillers Oxenfree and Oxenfree 2: Lost Signals.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Netflix is shuttering its Los Angeles-based game studio Night School, best known for side-scrolling psychological thrillers Oxenfree and Oxenfree 2: Lost Signals.

The streamer is also shutting down Moonloot, its game studio based in Helsinki, Finland, which has not yet released any titles but was developing an unannounced life-sim project.

Speaking with GameFile, a Netflix spokesperson confirmed the company still intends to release games on its platform, saying this latest move was an effort to streamline these efforts.

“We see an opportunity to be more focused in our execution, so we are making organizational changes to the business to match those priorities,” the spokesperson said. “We are incredibly grateful to the talented colleagues we’re saying goodbye to today. We thank them for all their contributions to Netflix, and wish them the best. Games continue to be an opportunity for us to expand the variety of entertainment we offer Netflix members.”

This news comes just after Night School released Unhinged, a first-person, narrative-driven horror game created in collaboration with Weapons director Zach Cregger, on June 30. Starring names like Sadie Sink and Zoë Kravitz, it stood out as a unique offering in the current gaming landscape, which reviewers described as a “fun and scary choose-your-own-adventure” romp.

A former member of Night School staff spoke about the closure on LinkedIn, writing, "Despite directing Unhinged and shipping it 6 weeks ago to millions of excited, satisfied players, it looks like I'm back on the market (along with the rest of Night School Studio)! ...I'm so proud of what we accomplished, and millions of people agree that we made a great product! Onward to the next exciting thing!"

These are the latest game studio closures from Netflix after the streamer shut down Team Blue in 2024. Netflix founded the developer in 2022, and it closed without releasing any games. It also closed Boss Fight Entertainment in 2025 after acquiring it in 2022, releasing several games within that timeframe. At the time, Netflix described Boss Fight’s closure as part of a “less-is-more strategy on a few identified verticals.”

Despite these most recent closures, Netflix has had positive things to say about its foray into the gaming space, with co-CEO Greg Peters saying Unhinged became one of its “most successful cloud game debuts” that yielded “really solid numbers that put it in the top tier of game performance for us” in a July 2026 investor call.

“We're scratching the surface in terms of what we think the total potential of the space offers for us. You're going to see us continue to calibrate and refine our level of investment here, which is still very small relative to our overall content spend based on demonstrated performance based on what is working for our members and what's delivering returns to our business,” he added.

items.title: Satechi’s New Six-Port USB-C Desktop Charger Offers 240W of Power
items.author: Wes Davis
items.content:
Satechi has released the ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger, a compact desktop charging brick with six USB-C ports that outputs enough power to keep your favorite power-hungry handheld gaming PC, gaming laptop, smartphone, and more topped up all at once. It even has a screen for those who want to see just how much their gear is drawing.

That 240W is a measure of the device’s total output, not any one USB-C outlet, but Satechi’s new charger can still push out 140W from either of its first two front-facing ports. That’ll charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed and is more than enough to max out the capacity of any handheld gaming PC you throw at it. The 240W Desktop Charger can also offer up to 100W on its second two ports, and up to 30W on the last two. Altogether, it has more ports and faster charging than most of IGN's current favorite USB-C chargers, both in general and for specific devices like the Steam Deck.

Satechi says its display can show the real-time power draw from each port, and that the charger “auto-detects each device’s requirements and balances output across active ports, keeping everything charged efficiently, quietly, and without overheating.” The product comes with a stand that lets you both rest the Desktop Charger horizontally or vertically, with a slight tilt so it’s easier to see the display. The charger comes in one color, Space Black.

The ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger costs $150 and is available now at Satechi’s website and Amazon.

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

items.title: 'It Doesn't Make Sense' — Uncharted Designer Doesn't Want a Remake of Drake's Fortune
items.description: Benson Russell, designer for two of the original Uncharted games, explained why he’s hesitant to welcome a potential remake of Drake’s Fortune.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Benson Russell, designer for two of the original Uncharted games and a current developer at Naughty Dog, explained why he’s hesitant to welcome a potential remake of Drake’s Fortune.

Uncharted: Drake’s Fortune released in 2007 on the PlayStation 3. It’s the first game in the original Uncharted trilogy and a title that studios still take inspiration from to this day, even two decades later.

Over the last two years, rumors have surfaced claiming that Naughty Dog is considering a remake of the iconic game. While this was mere speculation, players finally got to hear straight from the horse’s mouth in August 2026 when Benson Russell, designer for Drake’s Fortune and Uncharted 2: Among Thieves, spoke out about the subject in a conversation with FRVR.

For Russell, remakes don’t make sense if the original games are still part of the cultural zeitgeist, making the idea of a Drake's Fortune remake something of an uncessary task in his view.

“Uncharted as a thing is still in the zeitgeist,” he told the outlet. “System Shock… a remake of that now makes a lot of sense, because not just can you play it, but it had horrible key bindings, it kept a lot of people out of it from wanting to play it. There’s already a version [of Drake’s Fortune] you can play on modern consoles [to] get the experience. What’s the point of remastering [or remaking] it?”

“I just don’t see the point of remaking [it],” he continued. “You’d have to rewrite the whole story to make it better, which means you’re going to change the spirit and you’re going to change the scenes and what the first one was about, right? You’re going to have to add all these scenes or take things away and a lot of the key set pieces — are you going to keep those? Are you going to have to redo them because they don’t fit your story? It doesn’t make any sense [to remake it]. I honestly thought the same thing about The Last of Us Part 1… these are old games for a reason.”

Russell finished his spiel by saying a remake of Drake’s Fortune would feel “more like a cash grab than it would feel like anything necessary at this point,” saying, “Just don’t recreate the first game. It’s just, eh.”

While it’s currently unclear if Naughty Dog truly has any plans to work on a remake of Drake’s Fortune, it seems like all hands are on deck for the studio’s next title, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, which saw boss Neil Druckmann step away from his involvement in HBO’s The Last of Us series to better focus on. However, rumors of a Last of Us 3 game are also swirling around in the ether after Druckmann made a few comments online that hinted at another potential entry in the critically-acclaimed series.

items.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Is the Fastest Film to Reach $700 Million at Domestic Box Office
items.description: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is still on a tear at the box office, becoming the fastest movie to ever hit $700M domestically.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is still on a tear at the box office, becoming the fastest movie to ever hit $700M domestically.

Spidey’s latest adventure on the big screen is proving to be a major hit among moviegoers. It’s already dethroned Avengers: Endgame to snag the biggest opening weekend in domestic box office history, and now, it’s broken yet another massive record.

As of August 13, 2026, Spider-Man: Brand New Day has officially become the fastest movie to surpass $700M at the domestic box office. As of Wednesday, August 12, it had raked in $704.5 million, just under two weeks after its opening weekend.

As per The Hollywood Reporter, Brand New Day currently sits at sixth place in the list of highest-grossing films within North America. In terms of the top grossing films of all time, however, it currently sits somewhere between 10th and 8th place, between Zootopia 2 and Inside Out 2.

At the global box office, Spider-Man is swinging close to the $2 billion mark, surpassing $1.8 billion as of August 13. Alongside Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, both Tom Holland and Zendaya have had a massive run at the cinema this year — Zendaya especially, given her starring role alongside Robert Pattinson in The Drama in April and her upcoming appearance in Dune Part 3 (a film that also features Pattinson) in December.

Brand New Day’s success isn’t limited to the cinema; the film’s release also saw a huge surge in sales for Insomniac’s Spider-Man 2 game, with 316,000 copies getting sold as interest piqued among Marvel fans, translating to a jaw-dropping $11 million in sales across both PlayStation and Steam.

Critically, Brand New Day has been met with generally favorable reviews. IGN’s Tom Jorgensen scored the flick a 7 out of 10, remarking that it “effectively refocuses on the most reliable pillars of the webslinger: battling inner turmoil, swinging around NYC saving the day, and looking cool while doing so.”

items.title: Matthew McConaughey Explains Why He Turned Down Playing Joel in HBO's The Last of Us Show
items.description: Matthew McConaughey opened up about being approached to star as Joel in HBO’s The Last of Us series and why he had to turn it down.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Matthew McConaughey opened up about being approached to star as Joel Miller in HBO’s The Last of Us series and revealed why he had to turn the opportunity down.

In an August 13 episode of his Happy Sad Confused podcast, entertainment journalist Josh Horowitz mentioned that Craig Mazin — the co-creator, showrunner, and executive producer of The Last of Us show — had brought up the project to McConaughey early in its development.

The actor confirmed that this discussion took place, but said he wasn’t able to take the role at the time, as he was more focused on writing and felt some hesitation toward being involved in long-term projects like TV shows.

“I wasn’t really acting at that point,” he explained. “I think that was when I was doing more writing and looking at leadership roles. It was really good. He [Craig Mazin] was really excited. Correct me if I’m wrong — I’m not a huge TV watcher, but we pulled off a real coup with True Detective at a time when series were not something that actors like myself and Woody Harrelson would hop off and go do. That one succeeded in a real royal fashion.

“The Last of Us was really good, it wasn’t for me at the time. I don’t know what would’ve been for me at the time. I guess the first thing I came across was [The Rivals of Amziah King], that I went like, ‘Oh, this is extremely particular. It’s a movie. It’s one movie. A series, I do consider, ‘Well, you want this to succeed, and in its success, this is something you’ll be doing for years and years and years.’ Do I want that to be the case?”

This isn’t the first time the actor’s early discussions with Mazin have been brought up on Horowitz’s podcast; Mazin himself spoke about the talks in 2023, saying he floated the idea to McConaughey with Joel in mind, though it wasn’t anything super serious.

“I did talk to Matthew [McConaughey],” Mazin confirmed. “I can’t say it was serious. It was more like, ‘Hey, here’s something we can talk about.’ It’s one of those things where, I’m sure there’s an alternate universe where it’s a different actor. Matthew McConaughey is an amazing actor, I’m sure it would’ve been great, but it would’ve been different, and I like the one that we made.”

In the end, Pedro Pascal took on the mantle of Joel, a casting decision that turned out to be a major hit with both fans and critics alike. Mazin admitted that Pascal was already at the top of their list in the very beginning, but wasn’t sure he’d be available to take the part.

“As we were floundering about a little bit,” he told Horowitz. “I got a call from his agent who said, ‘You know, he actually might be available,’” Mazin said. “Normally when you send scripts off to actors like this, you’re lucky if you get a read within a month. He was in England at the time working on a movie and I thought between the movie and the time change, this will be forever. I sent it on Friday. Saturday morning I get a call: ‘He loves it. He wants to get on a Zoom.’”

While Season 1 of HBO’s The Last of Us adaptation was met with praise all around, Season 2 was decidedly less well-received, with viewers largely taking issue with how Ellie was portrayed in comparison to her video game counterpart.

Naughty Dog chief Neil Druckmann has stepped away from his involvement in the show to focus on the studio’s next game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet. The Last of Us will receive a third and final season — something that fans believe will also line up with a third game sometime down the line, if Druckmann’s previous comments are anything to go by.

items.title: 'Halo Studios Went Too Far in the Wrong Direction' — Co-Creator of Halo Hits Out at the Main Menu Ring in Xbox's New Remake
items.description: One of the creators of Halo has issued a few choice words for Xbox’s latest remake of Combat Evolved, specifically the ring we see in the main menu and the lack of PvP.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
One of the creators of Halo has issued a few choice words for Xbox’s latest remake of Combat Evolved, specifically the ring we see in the main menu and the lack of PvP.

Marcus Lehto was one of the key people behind the creation of Halo at Bungie, and while he left the studio a long time ago, he is still a popular figure among fans of the first-person shooter franchise. So when Lehto took aim at a Halo ring in the recently released Halo: Campaign Evolved, fans took notice.

“While Forerunner tech was metal (not stone) it was also ancient, vast, alive, and a tomb to the horrors that lurked within,” he began in a series of tweets on X. “It had seen hundreds of millennia of conflict. Yet the game shows it as shiny metal that looks like it was built a few years ago."

While Forerunner tech was metal (not stone) it was also ancient, vast, alive, and a tomb to the horrors that lurked within. It had seen hundreds of millennia of conflict. Yet the game shows it as shiny metal that looks like it was built a few years ago. pic.twitter.com/omp8Pwp76p

— Marcus Lehto (@game_fabricator) August 13, 2026

"The main menu ring is the most offensive thing we see every time we boot up the game. It should feel massive, dark, mysterious, sinister, but also full of wonder. This new ring looks like a shiny new toy - out of scale, no mystery, damn ugly.

“Also, for the lore, the ring in CE resides far out on the fringe of the Milky Way galaxy, which we see in the background."

Lehto continued: "What about war, flood outbreaks, repairs, collision? Also, the biggest issue is just with pure scale of the design. It lacks all the micro detail that should give it the epic scale it deserves. Lastly, it needs to feel like an ancient tomb."

This became a significant talking point within Halo circles, with some offering an explanation of sorts. The thought was that the sense of scale wasn’t being portrayed properly here, not just because more detail leaves less to the imagination, but because of where we view the ring from.

Lehto also agreed with a common complaint about Halo: Campaign Evolved — the lack of split-screen PvP. “There's little excuse aside from lack of oversight and poor planning that led to this misstep,” Lehto said. “So sad this wasn't included.”

However, it sounds like Lehto is a fan of the campaign itself. "Finished the fight on Heroic and honestly loved my playthrough of Halo: Campaign Evolved," he tweeted. "It was simultaneously a blast from my own past and fresh re-envisioning of the game I helped create. Perfect, no. Fun, absolutely yes!"

Halo: Campaign Evolved has sold 1.2 million copies across Xbox, PlayStation 5, and Steam, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics. It’s been out for two weeks. Alinea's Rhys Elliott called the sales figures "soft" so far, citing a lack of value and competitive multiplayer. “At the very least, if the rumored Halo 2 remake ships with online multiplayer, it’ll sell a great deal more, assuming it comes to PlayStation at all,” Elliott said.

Lehto’s comments aren’t even the first time Halo: Campaign Evolved sparked concern from a former Halo developer. In October last year, Jaime Griesemer, one of the key developers behind Halo, did not sound impressed when he reacted to the Halo: Campaign Evolved reveal, saying: “I made it right and they are breaking it for no reason.”

items.title: Krispy Kreme Is Getting 6 New Pokémon-Themed Donuts
items.description: Krispy Kreme has announced a Pokémon doughnut collection that will be available for a limited time starting August 18.
items.author: Blythe Dujardin
items.content:
Krispy Kreme has announced a Pokémon doughnut collection that will be available for a limited time starting August 18.

The collection, which is exclusive to U.S. and Canadian locations, will include six doughnuts total. Five are themed after specific Pokémon, including all three Gen 1 starters and two more Kanto region favorites. The sixth doughnut is an interpretation of the classic Poké Ball.

The doughnuts will be available for purchase individually or as a ‘Specialty Dozen Pack’ in select Krispy Kreme stores and through the Krispy Kreme app. A separate six-pack that skips out on Squirtle and Bulbasaur, replacing them with plain glazed doughnuts, will be available at other retailers like Walmart, Kroger, and Publix.

If you opt for the full Specialty Dozen, you’ll get a special, limited-edition Pokémon box. Krispy Kreme will also be offering five different Pokémon-themed cups for serving 'Original Glazed Gold Dots,' its version of doughnut holes.

That’s not all. Next Saturday, August 22, anyone who wears Pokémon merch to a participating Krispy Kreme location will get a free original glazed doughnut. It would have been nice if the freebie was Pokémon-themed, but a deal is a deal.

Krispy Kreme x Pokémon Doughnuts

  • Bulbasaur Doughnut – an Original Glazed® doughnut dipped in vanilla flavored icing and topped with frosting and a Bulbasaur piece.
  • Charmander Doughnut – an unglazed shell doughnut with chocolate and toasted marshmallow flavored filling, dipped in orange colored caramel icing and sparks of red and gold sugar, topped with a Charmander piece.
  • Squirtle Doughnut – an Original Glazed® doughnut piped with cotton candy flavored buttercreme, dipped in sanding sugar and nonpareils, and topped with a surfing Squirtle piece.
  • Pikachu Doughnut – an unglazed shell filled with lemon flavored Kreme™ filling dipped in vanilla icing, decorated with electrifying drizzle and nonpareils, and topped with a Pikachu piece.
  • Jigglypuff Doughnut – an Original Glazed® doughnut piped with strawberry flavored buttercreme, sprinkled with strawberry flavored cookie, and topped with a Jigglypuff piece.
  • Poké Ball Doughnut – an Original Glazed® doughnut dipped in vanilla flavored icing and red sprinkles, piped with chocolate icing.

Preorders for the full 12-pack have already opened online, suggesting the doughnut company may have some concerns about potential stock. Yes, the Pokémon scalping problem now extends far beyond the trading card game. This may explain why a press release from Krispy Kreme only indicates that the Pokémon-themed collection will be available for a ‘limited time’ instead of having a clear end date.

If you'd like to plan your Pokémon journey sooner rather than later, you can check for participating locations on the Krispy Kreme website.

The Krispy Kreme collection is the latest addition to a long list of Pokémon’s 30th anniversary celebrations. Throughout 2026, we’ve seen merch collaborations with companies like Puma, some beautiful new guide books, and the release of a whopping 20 Pokemon-themed LEGO sets. The Pokémon trading card game will also be getting a special 30th anniversary product drop later this year.

While we won’t be getting a mainline Pokémon game, we did get our first look at Gen 10, Winds and Waves, which is slated for 2027. We also got our hands on a new spin-off, Pokemon Pokopia, a Switch 2 exclusive we called an “enjoyable, personality-packed building simulator ” in our 9/10 review.

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

items.title: Game of Thrones: War for Westeros Gameplay Reveal Shows Lannister Troops Getting Cooked by a Fire-Breathing Dragon, With a Longer Look Due Later This Month
items.description: Here's a first look at gameplay for Game of Thrones: War for Westeros, the upcoming real-time strategy title that lets you conqueror the Seven Kingdoms on your own terms.
items.author: Tom Phillips
items.content:
Here's a first look at gameplay footage from Game of Thrones: War for Westeros, the upcoming real-time strategy title that lets you conqueror the Seven Kingdoms on your own terms.

Want a different ending to Game of Thrones? You're not alone, and happily you don't need to be when playing War for Westeros either — as you can capture the Iron Throne solo with a different or against others in multiplayer.

Today's glimpse shows a horde of soldiers dressed in red and holding Lannister banners, charging forward into battle. But oh, what's this? A gigantic shadow of a dragon flying overhead? I wonder what will happen next! Ah well, it is barbecue season.

Previous teases have confirmed that many of the characters and houses you'd expect will be included in the game, including Jon Snow and the armies of House Stark, Jamie Lannister and his forces, Daenerys and her dragons, and even the Night King.

Last month, Game of Thrones: War for Westeros developer PlaySide Studios pushed back the game's release window from 2026 into early 2027, explaining that the extra breathing room "gives us the time needed to continue building towards that goal and ensure that the game reaches the high level of quality we are aiming for."

"We remain unwavering in our mission to deliver a real-time strategy game set in the world of Westeros that meets the expectations of both RTS players and Game of Thrones fans," PlaySide added. "Thank you for your patience and continued support. We know the wait has been long, and we do not take your support for granted."

Today's brief but flame-grilled taste is really just designed to highlight a fuller gameplay reveal coming on August 25, as part of Gamescom Opening Night Live. Tune in then to see much more of the game, and as ever, IGN will be reporting from the event as it happens.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

items.title: Everything New We Learned About Marvel's Wolverine From Our Big Interview With Insomniac
items.description: Everything new we learned about Marvel's Wolverine from our big interview with Insomniac.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
We recently got the chance to sit down with developers from Insomniac to talk about PlayStation 5 exclusive Marvel’s Wolverine, and learned a whole lot about the studio’s approach to making the game, what fans can expect, and what is — and isn’t — included. Our interview with Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Insomniac, and Jess Reiner-Reed, senior project director, is below. We also went hands-on with Marvel’s Wolverine, and you can check out our impressions of the game ahead of its release on September 15, 2026.

There’s a lot to dig into here, so we thought it would be helpful to round up all our articles so you don’t miss a thing. And while you’re here, check out the latest Marvel’s Wolverine screenshots and our video preview, all embedded below.

Wolverine’s suit heals, too — here’s why

One of the big talking points coming out of the June State of Play gameplay reveal for Marvel’s Wolverine revolved around Logan’s suit healing alongside his body. This caused quite the kerfuffle within the community, with some fans saying it looks silly. We asked Insomniac why.

Sabretooth is a real jerk

Sabretooth, as Marvel fans know, is a jerk, but he’s an even bigger jerk when Wolverine’s around. The long-running rivalry between the two mutants is the stuff of comic book legend, but Insomanic brings it to life in its upcoming video game by forcing the two traditional adversaries to team up. Here’s how it works.

What adds replay value in Marvel’s Wolverine?

Insomniac told us all about the various features in Marvel's Wolverine designed to keep people playing after the credits roll. One in particular sounds like a proper nightmare.

Why don’t the X-Men Don't Exist in Marvel's Wolverine?

Don’t expect to see the X-Men in Marvel’s Wolverine — they don’t exist at this point in Wolverine’s story. But why? Insomniac explains.

How does Marvel's Wolverine run on base PS5?

Marvel's Wolverine has performance and fidelity modes, as you'd expect. But the performance mode on PS5 is particularly impressive. Here's why.

Marvel’s Wolverine: the final preview

We went hands-on with Marvel’s Wolverine. Here’s what we thought.

And here's our Marvel's Wolverine interview with Insomniac in full

IGN: I just want to get the general reaction to what the moment was where you learned that Wolverine was going to be your next project. What excited you about the project and was there anything that you foresaw being a challenge that you'd eventually have to overcome?

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah. So I started working on Marvel's Wolverine right as we were shipping Spider-Man: Miles Morales in November 2020. And it was beyond exciting to be able to think about what are we going to now work on with this character? You're telling a whole new fresh Logan-centric story. I had been working on Spider-Man 1 and Miles Morales for years at that point. So being able to think about, we're going to now be making a rated mature game, going to have claws and killing enemies, and exploring a character with a lot of depth. He's a quiet dude with a lot of mystery behind him. Yeah, I was nothing but excited when I found out we were working on Wolverine.

Mike Fitzgerald: Yeah. I think there was a little bit of, we'd been working with Spider-Man and Ratchet and Clank. These are really positive, warm and fuzzy characters. Warm and fuzzy are not two adjectives I would use for Logan. So it was a fun exercise for the studio to find, what is there about this character that matches the Insomniac spirit? What is his flavor of heroism that's different from those guys and how do we identify with that?

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah. He's not somebody who's going to be quipping nonstop and having fun jokes at the end of every fight. So yeah, like Mike's saying, it was really exploring what's that story we want to tell with this character?

IGN: So you just talked about the differences of going from Spider-Man to Wolverine. Were there any design lessons or decisions that you were able to carry over from your work on Spider-Man and bring them to Wolverine? Or did you see Wolverine as an opportunity to do a clean slate and do something different in the superhero space?

Mike Fitzgerald: I think the main lesson you could say we took through is that understanding the character deeply, what makes that character resonate with people. Even people who've experienced different versions of that character over time, finding the core of it and putting the player in a position to fulfill that fantasy thoroughly is the most important goal you can have. So learning about Wolverine, working with the folks at Marvel Games to understand, what about this character is core to him and making sure we live up to that.

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah. I think going back to your earlier question about what was that kind of early development learning about Wolverine? Obviously rated mature, violent. I was just remembering, I think realizing that Spider-Man doesn't kill enemies. All the enemies get web to the side of the buildings. Now Logan can actually take out enemies. So you can have that battlefield aftermath and really get to explore what that combat space can be. That was fantastic early on.

IGN: Was that kind of like a liberating feeling to not have to worry about enemies dying?

Jess Reiner-Reed: It was nice to be able to finally knock an enemy off a roof and have them die! Yeah, definitely. But I'd say, game development is a very iterative process. We get better at what we're doing over the course of every single game. So there's always learning lessons, not to sound too corny, but there's always learning lessons from each game that we can take. So there's a lot of Insomniac DNA in Marvel's Wolverine from what we learned from Spider-Man. But it was also, what would Logan do was really the core question we were asking every time. Not like, "Oh, how can we repurpose something from Spider-Man?" No, what would be right at the foundation for Logan?

IGN: Combat is obviously a huge part of this game. When it came to designing Wolverine's combat, what were some of the core pillars of design that you wanted to make sure that you nailed in terms of it being the power fantasy of being Wolverine?

Jess Reiner-Reed: So when working on the combat in Wolverine, you want to make sure that it feels brutal. You want to make sure that it feels aggressive. Wolverine's somebody who, he's not going to go run and hide in the corner and wait for his health to go up or anything. You're incentivized to have that aggression and keep fighting different enemies. We wanted to make sure to get his rage. So that's a core part of Logan, is he has this animalistic berserker rage and we wanted to make sure that came across in our game mechanics in combat. I hope you got to play part of that today where, when you get to rage tier three, you are just taking out enemies. He's almost blinded with rage and all he can see is the enemies in front of him.

The other parts we wanted to make sure to get right as far as Wolverine is his enhanced senses. So he's a tracker. He can, especially in stealth situations, you can start to see where enemies are, where a normal human wouldn't be able to notice that. Obviously his claws and adamantium skeleton. His healing, that was one of the things early in development of like, cool, how do you make a game around a guy who can constantly be healing? And I think that really came across in what we built.

Logan's good at fighting one enemy. He can probably take two enemies out. Once he starts to get swarmed and there's a hoard of enemies, that's where things start to be a problem for Logan. So we see that in our gameplay.

Mike Fitzgerald: Over the course of development, I think we learned a lot to say, okay, healing factor. I think on the surface that feels really easy to do in a video game. Yeah, you have a health bar and so the health bar is going to go up a bunch. But really trying to think about, okay, this is a unique piece of our character. What can we do in the gameplay that reflects that in a unique way? So players are thinking about, oh yes, this would only be in a Wolverine game. So something like the last stand moment where you use that rage you've built up during gameplay to sort of regenerate. You can see his body regenerate. You can see the damage he takes over the course of combat and sort of feeling that push and pull of his healing factor as you play.

IGN: Speaking of that healing factor, I have to bring up when you guys revealed some of the gameplay in June, one of the conversations that came out of that reveal was his regenerating clothing. No. Do you have a explanation for that or is there an in-game lore reason? What was going on with that?

Mike Fitzgerald: I think there might be something in there! I think mostly there's some practicalities to it. You can't play through most of the game wearing just shredded rags on his body. So we find the right balance between clothing that reflects the gameplay you're doing and this brutal combat and the realities of that. And then finding the right moments to have it restore itself so you get that right cinematic feel of Wolverine.

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah, exactly what you said. The right balance, because early on you would be playing through missions and your clothes are shredded for way too long. You don't feel as powerful as you're playing through. So yeah, we definitely found that right balance was the right thing to say.

IGN: Was it challenging coming up with all those different suits that he can wear, but also having to have damage go for each of those suits?

Mike Fitzgerald: Yeah, it's a unique thing for this game is as we develop each suit, we have to make this whole damage pipeline and process for each that show damage in different ways. But maybe more of the challenge is just deciding which not to do. There's so many fantastic Wolverine suits through the comics. We get to make some original ones with Marvel games as well. And so it's always a fun part of the development process, is arguing about which ones we actually want.

Jess Reiner-Reed: I love the suits we ended up with in game. I think in the press demo you played, we have the Weapon X suit, which is probably my favorite one with the helmet and everything. But we wanted to make sure that there's a lot of player choice with what suit and what claws you're going to be choosing, and we needed to have the damage reflect on all of those. So I'm glad you noticed that.

IGN: One of the things I wanted to touch on was these team up opportunities where you go into battle with Jean Grey or Sabretooth. Where did that come out of? And are there any other characters that players can look forward to doing these team ups with?

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah. So in the footage we've shown and the gameplay we've shown so far, I think today in our trailer there's a moment where Logan and Sabretooth are fighting together. Logan's holding a trash guard and Sabretooth is just ripping him apart. And then as you mentioned in the June footage, I think from State of Play, we had the different kind of ally cooperative moves with Jean Grey. Those came from a few different spots, but those are just really fun and you feel that connection with the other character as you're playing. I love those moments. And there's more you haven't seen, but I don't want to spoil anything. So yes, there are.

But one I want to mention is Sabretooth. You may have not seen it because it kind of randomly happens, but sometimes Sabretooth steals your kill. So you'll be in the middle of taking out an enemy and he like, wrecking ball grabs the enemy and takes him out. And the first couple of times you're like, "What the hell, Sabretooth?" But then you're like, "Wait, that's the exact feeling we want the player to..." Logan has this animosity with Sabretooth. And it's like, "Yeah, way to go guy. You just took my kill. Thanks." So yeah, I love some of those moments we have in there.

But conversely, Jean Grey, holding up with TK and then you being able to take out an enemy. Those feel great.

IGN: We've seen a lot of iconic takes on Wolverine. We've seen Hugh Jackman, Cal Dodd, Steve Blum. What do you think makes Liam McIntyre's portrayal stand out among what's already been done with the character?

Jess Reiner-Reed: He's Australian!

Mike Fitzgerald: We talk about Spider-Man as a character. He's sort of very outgoing. He says what he feels. Wolverine as a character is much more internal. You have to read a lot on his face. You have to read into what he's saying and the tone in which he's saying it. You have to get across this sort of rage-filled, animalistic exterior, and then also a very soft emotional interior as well. And Liam does a fantastic job representing both those things. We invested quite a bit to make sure we could reflect that in the game as well.

Jess Reiner-Reed: Yeah, he has that nuanced emotions. We scanned Liam, so every emotion you see, every growl and everything is coming from Liam. And if you get a chance to meet him, he's a fantastic guy in person to collaborate with. He loves games. And he's also one of the nicest humans I've met. So it's very different to then see him switch into his Logan role.

I'd say also when we were casting for Wolverine, what Liam brought to that character is he wasn't coming in being like, "I'm Wolverine." He wasn't like putting on a character. He just was. We also went hands-on with Marvel’s Wolverine, and you can check out our impressions of the game ahead of its release on September 15, 2026.

There’s a lot to dig into here, so we thought it would be helpful to round up all our articles so you don’t miss a thing. And while you’re here, check out the latest Marvel’s Wolverine screenshots and our video preview, all embedded below.

Wolverine’s suit heals, too — here’s why

One of the big talking points coming out of the June State of Play gameplay reveal for Marvel’s Wolverine revolved around Logan’s suit healing alongside his body. This caused quite the kerfuffle within the community, with some fans saying it looks silly. We asked Insomniac why.

Sabretooth is a real jerk

Sabretooth, as Marvel fans know, is a jerk, but he’s an even bigger jerk when Wolverine’s around. The long-running rivalry between the two mutants is the stuff of comic book legend, but Insomanic brings it to life in its upcoming video game by forcing the two traditional adversaries to team up. Here’s how it works.

What adds replay value in Marvel’s Wolverine?

Insomniac told us all about the various features in Marvel's Wolverine designed to keep people playing after the credits roll. One in particular sounds like a proper nightmare.

Why don’t the X-Men Don't Exist in Marvel's Wolverine?

Don’t expect to see the X-Men in Marvel’s Wolverine — they don’t exist at this point in Wolverine’s story. But why? Insomniac explains.

How does Marvel's Wolverine run on base PS5?

Marvel's Wolverine has performance and fidelity modes, as you'd expect. But the performance mode on PS5 is particularly impressive. Here's why.

Marvel’s Wolverine: the final preview

We went hands-on with Marvel’s Wolverine. Here’s what we thought.

items.title: Insomniac Confirms Marvel's Wolverine Performance Mode Details
items.description: Insomniac has revealed an impressive performance mode for Marvel’s Wolverine on the base PlayStation 5.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Insomniac has revealed an impressive performance mode for Marvel’s Wolverine on the base PlayStation 5.

Speaking to IGN, the Sony-owned developer said 60 frames-per-second with ray tracing is the default mode on base PS5 — a first for Insomniac.

“From early on in development, we knew we wanted to make this 60 FPS, working on the base PS5 in performance mode,” senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed said. “And we've definitely been able to accomplish that. The game feels super smooth.”

Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Insomniac, added: “We've always had these fidelity and performance modes, and then we always sort of last minute get the performance mode with ray tracing and like, ‘But this is pretty good...’ And so for this game from the start, we said, ‘You know what? We know we're confident we can ship this now. This is going to be a 60 frames per second game with ray tracing as the PS5 should have. We're going to build the game around this and towards this.’ And it's the default mode for the first time for us in one of our games. It’s important for the presentation.”

60 FPS with ray tracing as default on base PS5 is sure to go down well with players, especially considering the combat-heavy nature of Marvel’s Wolverine. Having that responsiveness is sure to help when it comes to nailing combos and tearing up enemies.

Elsewhere, Insomniac pushed the boat out when it comes to graphics performance in Marvel’s Wolverine, but it presented a very different opportunity compared to the Spider-Man games the developer is known for.

“Spider-Man's a very urban city based title,” Fitzgerald said. “We invest a lot in technology to represent that. And then Marvel’s Wolverine takes us outside the city. We spend some time in the wilderness of Canada, in a different nature of city in Madripoor. So we invested in a lot of tech around foliage and the jungles that you start the game in. All that foliage is very reactive to wind and characters and the environment going on around it.

“Logan's a really destructive character. The aftermath after you fight a big battle, we wanted to make sure you didn't feel like you were defeating a bunch of The Hand and then walking out of this pristine market that you happened to be in. So most of the props in the game are destructible, react in physically accurate ways. We invested a ton in that technology. So market stalls and tables and everything around you is splintering and flying off as you're doing combat.”

We've got plenty more on Marvel's Wolverine from our big interview with Insomniac. And don't forget to check out our hands-on preview ahead of the game's September launch.

items.title: Insomniac Explains Why Wolverine's Suit Heals Itself
items.description: Insomniac tells IGN why Wolverine's suit heals itself.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
One of the big talking points coming out of the June State of Play gameplay reveal for Marvel’s Wolverine revolved around Logan’s suit healing alongside his body. This caused quite the kerfuffle within the community, with some fans saying it looks silly.

"Wow, even his suit has a healing factor!" was one reaction to the gameplay. "NANOMACHINES, SON," another joked. Some have even suggested in-universe explanations for why Wolverine's suit heals itself (Reed Richards might have been involved!).

So, when we got the chance to sit down with Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Insomniac, and senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed to talk about all things Wolverine recently, we had to ask: what’s going on with Logan’s suit?

Rather than there being some deep cut lore explanation the developers drew from, Insomniac set out to achieve a balance between showing the effects of Wolverine's brutal combat and the practicality of the gameplay.

“I think mostly there's some practicalities to it,” Fitzgerald began. “You can't play through most of the game wearing just shredded rags on his body. So we find the right balance between clothing that reflects the gameplay you're doing and this brutal combat and the realities of that, and then finding the right moments to have it restore itself so you get that right cinematic feel of Wolverine.”

Reiner-Reed doubled down on this strive for a balance. “Early on you would be playing through missions and your clothes are shredded for way too long,” she said. “You don't feel as powerful as you're playing through. So yeah, we definitely found that right balance was the right thing to say.”

I’ve seen plenty of people say they would like to see suit damage remain, or progressively get worse. But let’s remember this is Wolverine we’re talking about. Given how much damage he takes, and how taking damage is kind of the way his combat works, he’d probably end up naked after about five minutes of action.

So, while suit damage does not hang about, Insomniac still had to create a damage pipeline and process for each suit in the game to show the damage that does occur in different ways.

"We invested a lot in how damage is reflected on him in his suit, on enemies and their suits," Fitzgerald explained. "And then as you attack them, the blood sprays coming off them are some really interesting fluid tech. So it's not just pre-baked visual effects. These are actual blood particles coming out. They hit the ground and make the exact splatter mark they would make if they land on Logan. They leave blood there. If he walks through water, it washes off and leaves blood swirls in the water."

We've got plenty more on Marvel's Wolverine from our big interview with Insomniac. And don't forget to check out our hands-on preview ahead of the game's September launch.
